repondus.texte: The seed is in the pods, not the flowers, so a spent bloom picked in June has nothing in it yet. Leave those plants where they are until fall, then collect pods once they start splitting open on their own. Scattering that seed on bare ground in October and covering it lightly is exactly the right method: winter gives it the cold spell it needs, and you get seedlings in spring without lifting a finger.

Yes to both. Wait until the pods crack open on their own, take the seed you want and let the rest fly; that is how the plant does it anyway. One thing worth knowing: milkweed seed needs roughly a month of cold before it will germinate, and a mild coastal winter does not always deliver that, so a sealed bag in the fridge for 30 days before spring sowing is good insurance. Expect leaves the first year and flowers the second.

Encouraging, and worth holding lightly: monarch counts swing hard from one year to the next, and one good season is not yet a trend. Twelve plants and a thousand seeds is a good position to be in. Two things worth knowing before you sow. Monarchs find a clump far more readily than the same plants scattered around a yard, so putting the new seed in as a patch will do more than the raw count suggests. And stored seed needs roughly 30 days of cold before it germinates, so either sow this fall and let winter do it, or give it a month in the fridge ahead of spring.

Maryland is easy country for this. The deciding factor is usually the spot rather than the state: ground that stays damp favours swamp milkweed (incarnata), a dry sunny bed favours butterfly weed (tuberosa), and common milkweed (syriaca) will take almost anything but travels underground, so it belongs somewhere you do not mind it spreading. None of the eleven species we carry is tropical milkweed. Before ordering, a Maryland native plant list is the better authority on what belongs in your county.

Yes. All eleven species we carry do well from roughly zone 3 through 9, so 8b sits comfortably inside that. Worth clearing up a common confusion while we are here: the zone on a seed packet is the coldest winter the plant will tolerate, not a ceiling. Being warmer than the listed zone is not the problem people assume it is.

Monarch Drive is a fitting address for this. Rocky and poor is closer to ideal than you would think: butterfly weed (tuberosa) sends down a deep taproot and does its best work in lean, well drained ground, the sort that frustrates most garden plants. It sulks in rich soil and hates wet feet, so a rough yard plays to its strengths. Full sun, then leave it alone once established. An Arkansas native plant list is worth a look too, so you know what already belongs on your street.

Worth checking a Missouri native plant list before ordering, since a local range map is more precise than anything we can tell you from here.

Stripped milkweed is the good sign rather than the bad one. That is the caterpillars doing precisely what the plant is there for, and being a native perennial it comes back from the roots each spring, often stronger than the year before. Sounds like your garden is already doing the work.

Almost always the same cause, and it is not you. Milkweed seed will not germinate without a cold spell first, roughly 30 days of it. Sown straight from the packet in spring, most of it simply sits there and rots. Sow in autumn and let winter do the work, or give it a month in the fridge before spring. Worth one more try on that basis.

Exactly right, and thank you for spelling it out. That cold period is the one step most people skip, and it is why so many packets get written off as duds. Ours are sold unstratified for precisely that reason, so the choice stays with the grower: the fridge, or an autumn sowing and let winter handle it.

Yes. Downeast winters sit well inside what these plants want, and the cold is an asset rather than an obstacle here: the seed needs a winter to break dormancy, so an autumn sowing does that work for free. Common milkweed and swamp milkweed both take that climate without complaint.

Swamp milkweed (incarnata) is the opposite temperament: ordinary garden soil suits it, and it is happiest where moisture lingers. Both do better in the ground than in pots if you have the room. Scattering works, with two conditions. The ground has to be bare enough that seed reaches actual soil instead of sitting on thatch, and it has to be autumn, so that winter delivers the cold spell the seed needs. Scattered onto untouched ground in spring, you will get very little. Sowing into pots gives better odds per seed, but an autumn scatter over a prepared patch is closer to what the plant does for itself.

What you mainly need is a sunny spot you can leave undisturbed for two years, since milkweed gives you foliage the first season and flowers only the second. Beyond that, your ground decides more than your zone does: butterfly weed (tuberosa) for a dry sunny bed, swamp milkweed (incarnata) where moisture lingers.
